title: The periodic table: who gives, who takes

concepts.label: period
concepts.definition: A row of the periodic table; the period number is the number of electron shells that hold electrons.

concepts.label: group
concepts.definition: A column of the periodic table (numbered 1–18); its members have the same number of valence electrons (group number for groups 1–2, group − 10 for groups 13–18).

concepts.label: noble gas
concepts.definition: A group-18 element (He, Ne, Ar, Kr …) with a full outer shell, which neither gives nor takes electrons.

concepts.label: alkali metal
concepts.definition: A group-1 element below hydrogen (Li, Na, K, Cs …) with one valence electron beyond a full shell, which it gives away easily to form a 1+ ion.

concepts.label: halogen
concepts.definition: A group-17 element (F, Cl, Br, I) one electron short of a full shell, which readily takes one electron to form a 1− ion.

concepts.label: ionisation energy
concepts.definition: The energy cost (kJ/mol) of removing the most loosely held electron from an isolated atom: X → X⁺ + e⁻; low for givers, high for takers and noble gases.

concepts.label: core charge (simplified)
concepts.definition: Protons minus inner-shell electrons: the net positive charge an outer electron feels in the simple shell model; with distance it explains why ionisation energy and electronegativity rise across a period and fall down a group.

concepts.label: electronegativity
concepts.definition: A unitless score (Pauling scale, about 0.8–4.0) for how strongly an atom pulls on electrons when it meets another atom; electrons drift toward the higher value and a large gap means transfer.

concepts.label: metal
concepts.definition: An element with low ionisation energy and low electronegativity (left and bottom of the table) that gives electrons and forms cations.

concepts.label: non-metal
concepts.definition: An element with high ionisation energy and high electronegativity (upper right of the table, plus hydrogen) that takes or shares electrons and forms anions.

concepts.label: typical ion charge
concepts.definition: The charge an element usually carries as an ion: metals lose all valence electrons (groups 1, 2, 13 → 1+, 2+, 3+), non-metals gain enough to fill the shell (groups 15, 16, 17 → 3−, 2−, 1−).

concepts.label: transition metal
concepts.definition: A metal in groups 3–12 (Fe, Cu, Zn …) with 1–2 outer electrons over a growing inner shell; usually forms 2+ ions and often has a second common charge (Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺, Cu⁺/Cu²⁺).

namedOnly: mole (kJ/mol used only as a unit for comparison; defined in Ions, salts and electrolytes)
semimetal / borderline elements (B, Si, Ge, As)
electron sharing / covalent bond (pointer to Silicon and light)
successive ionisation energies (shown as a chart, not named as a concept)
activity series (pointer: gold and platinum as reluctant givers)
summary: Running example: sodium and chlorine from Atoms, electrons and charge, now located in the table (group 1 vs group 17) and given numbers: ionisation energy 496 vs 1251 kJ/mol, electronegativity 0.93 vs 3.16, core charge +1 vs +7. The capstone is a full periodic table (all Chem.elements) recolourable by class, valence, ionisation energy, electronegativity or typical ion, plus a 'pick a giver and a taker' experiment that animates the electron transfer, sets the atom ratio so electrons given = electrons taken, and explains failures (two metals, two non-metals, noble gas, roles reversed). Hooks for later lessons: typical ion charges and the 'atoms team up until charges cancel' picture (ionic formulas), metals as givers with gold/platinum as reluctant ones (activity series), Li and F as the extreme giver and taker (electrode potentials), silicon as a fence-sitter that shares (solar cells), light elements giving several electrons (specific capacity).

Chem.elements could carry a metal / non-metal / semimetal class and the typical ion charge(s), so lessons agree on them (this lesson defines its own NONMETAL / SEMI / TYP tables).
